_comment: JOKES, BANTER AND LITTLE DIGS.
Asked for directly: "wheres the jokes and banter and little digs? its
nice to have some comedic moments on track". He is right — a booth with
no lightness in it is exhausting over an hour.
THE COST IS ASYMMETRIC, AND THAT SHAPES EVERYTHING HERE. A joke that
lands adds a little. A joke over a driver sitting in a wrecked car
destroys the illusion in one line and nothing said afterwards repairs it.
So `_levity_ok()` in overlay_booth.py is a HARD VETO checked before any
of these is offered: nothing funny after an incident, under a yellow, in
the closing laps, during the late phase of a title decider, or while the
player is damaged, off or in the pits.
WHO MAY BE THE JOKE, and this is the whole editorial rule:
THE TWO OF THEM        always. Miles and Chuck ribbing each other is
the safest and best comedy available, because
nobody in it is trying to drive a car.
THE SITUATION          always. Traffic, the weather, the length of the
race, the pit wall, the sport in general.
A DRIVER'S DRIVING     only when GROUNDED in something the booth has
actually observed and the viewer can see — a man
stuck behind the same gearbox for ten laps, a
man who has been off three times. Never a
generic insult, never about a result.
THE PLAYER             yes, and deliberately. Being off the pace is not
a misfortune, it is racing, and a booth that
never ribs the man driving is a press officer.
But `_levity_ok` refuses the moment he is
actually in trouble.
NEVER: a driver's nationality, appearance, age as an insult, intelligence,
or anything that would read as contempt rather than affection. These are
real people, several of them dead, and the booth likes all of them.
Chuck is a NASCAR Cup champion and Brett a WEC champion. Neither has
driven a Formula One car, so a joke may not rest on having done so —
`disc: ["stock"]` gates the ones that draw on Chuck's own racing.
LAW 14: every line stands alone. The bag may draw any of these first, so
nothing here may read as a reply to a line that has not aired.

booth_joke.t: I'd say that's brave, but I've seen you park worse.
You say that every race, and you've been right about twice.
That's the most excited I've heard you all afternoon.
In my day we called that a racing incident and bought a beer afterwards.
I'm told that is what the young drivers call commitment. There used to be a different word for it.
Somewhere there is an engineer watching that on a screen and quietly ageing.
That is a man who has decided the racing line is a suggestion.
Every single one of them thinks the car is the problem. Every single one.
I have never once heard a driver come in and say the setup was perfect and he simply drove badly.
There is a strategist on that pit wall drawing a chart nobody has asked for.
The trick is to sound certain. Nobody remembers what you predicted, only how confident you were.
Racing drivers and rear-view mirrors. Fitted as standard, used as decoration.
If everybody drove sensibly we would both be out of a job.
You can hear the radio message from here, and I would not repeat it.
There is no prize for being tidy. He seems to have read that somewhere.
I would call that optimistic. His engineer will use a different word.
A racing driver's memory is a wonderful thing. It only keeps the good laps.
Nobody in this sport has ever been at fault. It is remarkable, statistically.

booth_dig.t: Chuck, you have been quiet. Either you are thinking or you have gone to sleep.
That is the third time you have said that, Chuck. I am keeping count now.
I will take that as analysis, Chuck, because the alternative is that you just guessed.
You have a lovely way of explaining something after it has already happened.
Chuck, if you are right about this I will say so on air. If you are wrong we shall never mention it again.
You are enjoying this far too much for a man who is supposed to be neutral.
Careful, Chuck. Any more enthusiasm and somebody might think you missed racing.
Every week you tell me the tyres are the story. One of these days it will be something else.
Thank you, Chuck. That was almost an answer to the question I asked.
Say something clever, Chuck, they are paying you by the sentence.
You have been threatening to make a point for about a lap and a half now.
I hear you, Chuck, but you also said this would be dull.

analyst_dig.t: You are getting excited again. Breathe.
That is the voice you use when you have run out of things to say.
You have called three cars by the wrong name today. I am not going to say which.
I like that you say it with such confidence. It is almost persuasive.
You have never driven one of these and it has never once slowed you down.
I will answer that properly if you promise to stop shouting.
That is a question with no answer, and you know it, and you asked it anyway.
You are describing it beautifully. You are also describing it wrongly.
Give it a minute and you will have talked yourself into the opposite of that.
Every race you ask me that, and every race I tell you the same thing.
